title: AI Riemann Hypothesis proof is true, independent mathematicians confirm
content:
Editor's Note: This story was updated on Nov. 21 to reflect further confirmation of the proof.
Mathematicians are now certain the earth-shattering artificial-intelligence-created proof of the Riemann hypothesis is real.
On Friday Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge claimed to have used the company’s Claude AI model to solve the Riemann problem, perhaps the most important open quandary in mathematics. The hypothesis, first posed in 1859 by mathematician Bernhard Riemann, suggests that a hidden pattern underlies the distribution of the prime numbers—those numbers that are divisible only by themselves and 1.

Now researchers have verified that the proof does do what Alpöge claims.
"We have full confidence that Alpöge's proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct, and we congratulate him on this achievement," mathematicians wrote in a joint statement by the Lean and Mathlib communities, which support the Lean mathematics programming language. "We hereby certify that both the statement and the proof of the Riemann Hypothesis are correct."
Alpöge initially checked the work by writing out the proof using Lean; if a Lean-coded proof compiles error-free, this is usually taken as confirmation that the logic and math in each step is correct.
But some questions remained. For instance, does the proof really address the Riemann hypothesis, or does it establish a subtly different point or idea? “The first question which one has to ask when judging a PDF which comes with some Lean code is: ‘what is the statement of the theorem in the Lean code, and does this correspond to the actual theorem statement,’” explained mathematician Kevin Buzzard of Imperial College London in a blog post.
A second question was whether the Lean code would successfully compile for other mathematicians. Independent researchers, including Andrew Sutherland, a mathematician at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, have now separately compiled Alpöge’s result in Lean without issues.
“The Lean proof has been compiled and independently rechecked by the Lean kernel with only the three standard axioms,” Sutherland says. “Honestly the chance that anything is fishy here is approximately zero.”
Researchers also made sure that the proof does not include any hack, dodge or shortcut that changed the meaning of the initial hypothesis or any other mathematical rules or truths. This process, called a “comparator run,” typically takes a matter of hours.
“We still await a successful comparator run, which will check that (a) the code does not do anything nefarious like redefine the meaning of any of the symbols in the statement and (b) (assuming it’s run in paranoid mode) the code compiles with several independent kernels (so the code is not just exploiting an as yet unknown bug in Lean’s official kernel,” Buzzard wrote on an online chat server for the Lean community.
That run has now been completed.

report.summary: Independent mathematicians have certified that an AI-generated Lean proof of the 1859 Riemann hypothesis compiles correctly, potentially marking a landmark result in automated mathematics.
report.background: The Riemann hypothesis, first proposed by Bernhard Riemann in 1859, concerns the distribution of prime numbers—integers divisible only by themselves and 1. It posits a hidden regularity in how primes are spread across the number line, and it underpins large swaths of analytic number theory. It is one of the Clay Mathematics Institute's Millennium Prize Problems, unproven for more than 165 years. In recent years, AI systems have made inroads into olympiad-level and research mathematics, but trust has been the bottleneck: a plausible-looking proof can hide subtle errors. Formal proof languages such as Lean, whose Mathlib library encodes mathematics in machine-checkable form, offer a way out. If a Lean proof compiles without error, the logical steps are verified by a small trusted kernel. Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge reportedly used the company's Claude model to produce such a proof, then submitted it to the Lean and Mathlib communities for independent scrutiny.
key_points: Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge claimed to have used the Claude AI model to solve the Riemann hypothesis, then wrote the proof out in Lean, the formal mathematics programming language. The Lean and Mathlib communities issued a joint statement certifying that both the statement and the proof of the Riemann hypothesis are correct.

Verification focused on two questions: whether the Lean code actually states the Riemann hypothesis rather than something subtly different, and whether the code compiles on other mathematicians' machines. MIT mathematician Andrew Sutherland independently compiled it using only the three standard axioms, saying the chance of anything being wrong is approximately zero.

A 'comparator run' was performed to rule out hacks, dodges or redefinitions—checking that the code does not secretly redefine symbols in the theorem statement and, in paranoid mode, that it compiles across several independent kernels rather than exploiting an unknown bug in Lean's official kernel. That run has now completed.

The result, if it holds, would be the first time an AI system has contributed decisively to resolving one of mathematics' most famous open problems, shifting formal verification from a specialist curiosity to the central trust mechanism for machine-generated mathematics.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the result is a strong argument that formal verification—not human eyeballing—should be the acceptance test for AI-generated reasoning, with Lean and similar systems becoming the audit layer for trustworthy machine output. For developers and mathematically minded engineers, it elevates proof-engineering skills and tooling around Lean, Mathlib and kernel checking from niche to strategically valuable. For regular users, the immediate effects are indirect: the Riemann hypothesis does not break RSA or other practical cryptography, but progress on prime distribution feeds number theory, algorithm design and randomness, and the broader shift toward verifiable AI output could make claims from AI systems more checkable in medicine, software and law. Caveats remain: this is a single, freshly verified result, and independent replication across the wider community is still ongoing.
report.tools: To follow along, explore Lean 4 and its Mathlib library, the community hub for formalized mathematics, plus the Lean Zulip chat where verifiers coordinate. The Lean 4 playground is the easiest way to try small formalizations. Also watch AI-for-math systems such as Google DeepMind's AlphaProof and Harmonic's Aristotle, and comparator-style tooling that checks formal proofs against independent kernels—these are becoming the standard instruments for auditing AI-generated mathematics.
